news.title: IrisVision Ultra: unas nuevas gafas inteligentes amplían la visión hasta 10 aumentos con ayuda de la inteligencia artificial
news.summary: La compañía IrisVision presenta un nuevo dispositivo electrónico para personas con baja visión. Incorpora enfoque automático, diferentes modos de visualización y un asistente de inteligencia artificial capaz de leer textos y adaptar la imagen a las necesidades del usuario. La tecnología continúa ofreciendo nuevas alternativas para las personas con discapacidad visual. Una de las últimas […] La entrada IrisVision Ultra: unas nuevas gafas inteligentes amplían la visión hasta 10 aumentos con ayuda de la inteligencia artificial se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
La compañía IrisVision presenta un nuevo dispositivo electrónico para personas con baja visión. Incorpora enfoque automático, diferentes modos de visualización y un asistente de inteligencia artificial capaz de leer textos y adaptar la imagen a las necesidades del usuario.

La tecnología continúa ofreciendo nuevas alternativas para las personas con discapacidad visual. Una de las últimas novedades llega de la mano de IrisVision, que ha presentado sus nuevas IrisVision Ultra , unas gafas electrónicas diseñadas para facilitar actividades cotidianas como leer, reconocer rostros, ver la televisión o consultar información a distancia.

Uno de los principales atractivos de las IrisVision Ultra es su capacidad de ampliación. El dispositivo permite aumentar la imagen hasta 10 veces y cuenta con un sistema de enfoque automático que mantiene la nitidez al observar objetos a diferentes distancias.

Esto permite utilizar las gafas para distintas actividades, tanto de cerca como a distancias intermedias o lejanas.

Además, incorporan varios modos de visualización para adaptar la imagen a diferentes necesidades:

También incluyen un modo específico para televisión, que ajusta la exposición para reducir los reflejos y mejorar la visualización de los contenidos.

Otra de las novedades es la integración de Iris, la plataforma de inteligencia artificial de IrisVision.

Este asistente permite controlar diferentes funciones mediante comandos de voz. El usuario puede solicitar que aumente la imagen, modifique el brillo, cambie el contraste o active un modo de lectura.

Una de sus funciones más interesantes es la lectura de textos en voz alta. Basta con dirigir la mirada hacia una página, una etiqueta o una carta para pedirle a Iris que lea su contenido.

El sistema admite 14 idiomas, entre ellos el español, y permite interactuar con las gafas utilizando instrucciones sencillas.

La inteligencia artificial también facilita el acceso a otros contenidos. Por ejemplo, permite buscar vídeos en YouTube, consultar películas, escuchar audiolibros y acceder a juegos diseñados específicamente para personas con baja visión.

Las IrisVision Ultra pesan aproximadamente 230 gramos y ofrecen una autonomía de hasta 10 horas, según las condiciones de uso y la configuración del dispositivo.

Una de sus novedades es la incorporación de botones táctiles directamente en las gafas. Gracias a ellos, el usuario puede desplazarse por los diferentes modos, modificar los aumentos y controlar las funciones sin necesidad de manejar un mando independiente.

Esta característica resulta especialmente interesante desde el punto de vista de la accesibilidad, ya que permite localizar los controles mediante el tacto.

Además, cada dispositivo incluye una sesión individual de formación a distancia para ayudar al usuario a familiarizarse con sus funciones.

IrisVision presenta este dispositivo como una ayuda electrónica para personas con diferentes patologías visuales.

Entre los perfiles a los que se dirige se encuentran personas con:

Las diferentes opciones de ampliación, contraste y adaptación del campo visual permiten personalizar la experiencia según las necesidades de cada persona.

No obstante, estas gafas no son una solución universal. Su utilidad depende del resto visual, las características de cada patología y las necesidades concretas del usuario. Por eso, es recomendable probar el dispositivo y contar con asesoramiento especializado en baja visión antes de adquirirlo.

El precio es uno de los aspectos más importantes de este lanzamiento.

Según la página oficial del fabricante, las IrisVision Ultra tienen un precio promocional de 3.799 dólares , frente a los 3.999 dólares de su precio original.

Al cambio aproximado, esta cantidad equivale a unos 3.460 euros. Sin embargo, hay que tener en cuenta que se trata de una conversión orientativa y que el precio final para compradores europeos puede variar.

La compañía indica además un coste de envío internacional de 135 dólares. A esta cantidad podrían añadirse impuestos y otros gastos de importación, por lo que conviene consultar las condiciones antes de realizar el pedido.

Por el momento, el fabricante comercializa el dispositivo directamente desde su página web.

Las IrisVision Ultra representan una nueva apuesta por las ayudas electrónicas portátiles para personas con baja visión.

Su combinación de ampliación de imagen, ajustes de contraste, lectura de textos e inteligencia artificial busca facilitar actividades cotidianas que pueden resultar complicadas cuando existe una pérdida de visión.

Aunque su precio sigue siendo elevado y será necesario conocer la experiencia de los usuarios con este nuevo modelo, el dispositivo muestra cómo la tecnología puede ofrecer herramientas cada vez más personalizadas para aprovechar el resto visual.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuente: Iris Vision

news.title: From TalkBack to Jieshuo, and Now SandFly: My Journey Through Android Screen Readers
news.summary: After years of using TalkBack and Jieshuo, I’ve decided to make SandFly my primary screen reader. For me, this isn’t simply about replacing one application…
news.body:
Published 18 November 2026 by Salih Kunduz

After years of using TalkBack and Jieshuo, I’ve decided to make SandFly my primary screen reader.

For me, this isn’t simply about replacing one application with another. It’s also an opportunity to look back at how Android accessibility has evolved over the years, what we’ve gained along the way, and what I expect from a screen reader today.

I’ve been using Android for a long time, and I’ve witnessed quite a few changes in its accessibility ecosystem. Some were genuinely exciting, while others reminded us how limited our choices were.

Table of Contents

For much of the period between 2013 and 2020, TalkBack was practically the only realistic option for many blind Android users.

There were other attempts and alternatives, of course, but TalkBack dominated the ecosystem. It came with Google’s backing, was integrated into Android, and worked across a wide range of devices.

I don’t want to underestimate what TalkBack meant to us during those years. It made Android usable for millions of blind people, including me. It improved considerably over time, and many features we take for granted today were not available in its earlier versions.

However, there was always something that bothered me: performance.

TalkBack often felt heavier and slower than it needed to be. Navigating through interfaces, moving between elements, and performing everyday tasks sometimes required more patience than I thought was reasonable.

And when you use a screen reader for practically everything you do on your phone, these small delays add up.

The problem wasn’t simply that TalkBack was slow. It was that we had very little choice. If something didn’t work the way we wanted, we could report it, wait for an update, or learn to live with it.

For years, that was simply the reality of Android accessibility.

My experience with Jieshuo changed the way I thought about screen readers.

For the first time, I felt that I was getting much closer to the full performance of my Android device.

The difference wasn’t limited to speech responsiveness. Navigation felt faster, interactions were more immediate, and I had considerably more control over how my screen reader behaved.

Jieshuo offered a level of customization that TalkBack had never really provided. I could adjust the experience to suit my habits rather than constantly adapting my habits to the screen reader.

Once you become accustomed to that level of responsiveness and flexibility, going back isn’t easy.

But Jieshuo had its own problems.

One of the biggest challenges was communication with its developer. When something didn’t work properly, reporting an issue and getting meaningful feedback wasn’t always straightforward. For a product that plays such an important role in our daily lives, communication matters enormously.

There was also the issue of distribution and compatibility.

Because Jieshuo wasn’t available through Google Play, certain banking applications and other security-sensitive services occasionally created problems. Some applications treated the screen reader as a potential security risk, even though we were simply using it to access our devices.

As a blind user, I found that particularly frustrating.

A screen reader isn’t an optional convenience. It’s the interface through which we interact with our phones. Having to choose between using the screen reader I prefer and accessing essential services is not a reasonable situation.

And then there were the practical complications. Even something as ordinary as paying for a screen reader could involve additional services, intermediaries, or procedures that an average user shouldn’t have to deal with.

These things might seem relatively minor when considered separately, but together they affect the overall experience.

Jieshuo showed me what was possible in terms of performance and customization. At the same time, it made me appreciate certain advantages I had previously taken for granted.

Despite all my criticism of TalkBack’s performance, I never completely abandoned it.

There was something reassuring about knowing it was there.

TalkBack was officially supported, widely recognized, and generally less likely to create complications with applications that were sensitive to accessibility services.

Whenever I encountered a problem with Jieshuo, I knew I could return to TalkBack.

It might not have been as fast or as flexible as I wanted, but it provided a familiar and relatively predictable experience.

In that sense, TalkBack became my safe harbor.

And I think that says something important about screen readers. Performance matters, but so do stability, reliability, compatibility, and trust.

The ideal screen reader shouldn’t force us to sacrifice one for another.

After all these years, I think we need to reconsider what we actually expect from an Android screen reader.

Of course, responsiveness and advanced features matter. Nobody wants to use a slow or unnecessarily restrictive screen reader.

But speed alone isn’t enough.

A screen reader should be stable, reliable, and inclusive. It should be easy to obtain, straightforward to set up, and accessible to people with different levels of technical experience.

You shouldn’t need a master’s degree, let alone a PhD in technology, just to configure your screen reader and use your phone comfortably.

I enjoy experimenting with technology. I don’t mind exploring advanced settings, testing new features, or finding workarounds when something doesn’t behave as expected.

But that’s my personal interest. It shouldn’t be a requirement for everyone else.

Someone who has just started using Android with a screen reader should be able to learn the basics without feeling overwhelmed. Meanwhile, experienced users should have access to the advanced tools and customization they need.

These two expectations aren’t contradictory.

A well-designed screen reader should be approachable for beginners without becoming restrictive for advanced users.

Accessibility must extend beyond the application’s interface, too. Installation, updates, payments, documentation, and communication with developers are all part of the experience.

If obtaining or paying for an accessibility tool requires navigating through several third-party services and complicated procedures, then something is wrong with that experience.

These considerations have become increasingly important to me, and they’re among the reasons I’ve started looking at SandFly more seriously.

What initially attracted me to SandFly was its approach.

Because SandFly builds on TalkBack’s foundation, many aspects of the experience already feel familiar. Its settings, menus, and general structure don’t require me to forget years of accumulated habits and start from scratch.

That’s a significant advantage.

Changing screen readers isn’t always easy, particularly when you’ve spent years developing your own gestures, routines, and ways of interacting with Android.

With SandFly, I feel that I’m getting something close to the safety and familiarity of TalkBack, combined with a much more capable and comfortable environment.

If TalkBack was my safe harbor, SandFly feels like that same harbor opening into a much more luxurious bay.

It’s a slightly unusual comparison, perhaps, but it describes the feeling quite well.

The familiar foundation is still there, while the possibilities continue to expand.

SandFly is still a developing project, and I don’t want to pretend that every feature is perfect or that it has already solved every problem. However, its advanced capabilities are progressing, and I’ve been encouraged by the direction of its development.

Another important advantage is how approachable the experience feels.

I don’t have to spend hours trying to understand an entirely unfamiliar system just to configure the basics. At the same time, there are more advanced possibilities to explore as I become accustomed to it.

That balance is exactly what I want from a modern screen reader.

There are also some very practical reasons behind my decision.

First, paying for the software doesn’t have to become a separate technical challenge. If I decide to purchase it, I don’t have to deal with numerous intermediary services just to complete the process.

That might not sound particularly exciting, but simplicity matters.

Second, SandFly hasn’t caused problems with the banking service I personally use.

I want to be careful about how I describe this. My experience doesn’t mean every banking application will necessarily work without issues for every user. But for me, being able to use my preferred screen reader without compromising access to an essential financial service is a major advantage.

And then there’s something that deserves more attention: physical keyboards.

SandFly appears to place considerable importance on physical keyboard support, and it’s clear that thought has gone into this part of the experience.

This matters to me personally because I don’t use Android exclusively on a phone. I also use a tablet, and physical keyboard interaction is an important part of how I work with it.

A screen reader that treats physical keyboard navigation as a serious part of the user experience, rather than an afterthought, immediately becomes more interesting to me.

I don’t think physical keyboard support receives enough attention in discussions about Android accessibility.

We often focus on touch gestures, speech responsiveness, and customization. Those are important, of course, but Android is no longer limited to the traditional smartphone experience.

Tablets, foldables, keyboards, and different ways of interacting with our devices deserve equal consideration.

The more I explored SandFly from this perspective, the more I began to feel that it could become a screen reader I would genuinely enjoy using every day.

There’s another factor that has influenced my decision: communication with the developer.

After my experience with Jieshuo, I have come to value this much more than I used to.

Being able to contact a developer, explain a problem, discuss an idea, and receive feedback makes a real difference.

This doesn’t mean every suggestion should be accepted or every bug should be fixed immediately. Software development doesn’t work that way.

What matters is knowing that communication is possible and that users’ experiences are being considered.

Through my work with Accessible Android, I’ve spent a considerable amount of time testing applications, reporting accessibility issues, and communicating with developers.

One thing I’ve learned is that the relationship between developers and users can influence the quality of a product just as much as technical decisions do.

SandFly’s developer has been approachable, and that gives me another reason to follow the project closely.

Of course, good communication alone doesn’t guarantee good software. The product still has to demonstrate its reliability through daily use.

But when a project combines technical ambition with an approachable developer, I’m much more willing to invest my time in it.

I’m not switching to SandFly because I believe TalkBack has become irrelevant or because I want to dismiss everything Jieshuo has offered me.

Quite the opposite.

I appreciate what both screen readers have contributed to my Android experience.

Without TalkBack, my early years on Android would have been very different. Without Jieshuo, I might never have realized how much faster and more flexible screen reading could feel.

But I’m also not particularly interested in remaining loyal to a screen reader simply because I’ve used it for years.

My loyalty is to accessibility, independence, and the freedom to use technology in the way that suits me best.

SandFly will have to prove itself through everyday use. There will almost certainly be bugs, missing features, and situations where I may need to return to another screen reader.

That’s perfectly normal for a developing project.

For now, however, I see enough potential to make the transition.

What I find particularly encouraging is that we seem to be moving toward a more diverse Android accessibility ecosystem.

We no longer have to evaluate screen readers solely in terms of whether they can read an interface. We can discuss performance, usability, reliability, physical keyboard support, distribution, payment accessibility, developer communication, and the overall quality of the experience.

And we should.

After all, an Android screen reader shouldn’t simply make a device accessible.

It should make using that device comfortable, efficient, and enjoyable.

That’s what I’m looking for in SandFly, and that’s why I’ve decided to give it a chance.

news.title: Proyecto ABILITY: la IA que permite tocar gráficos y mapas
news.summary: La Unión Europea impulsa una innovadora tecnología que combina pantallas táctiles bidimensionales e inteligencia artificial. Gracias a este avance, las personas ciegas podrán explorar esquemas, mapas y documentos digitales en tiempo real. ¿Qué es exactamente el proyecto ABILITY y por qué importa? El proyecto ABILITY (Accessible Digital Services for Blind and Partially Sighted People) es […] La entrada Proyecto ABILITY: la IA que permite tocar gráficos y mapas se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
La Unión Europea impulsa una innovadora tecnología que combina pantallas táctiles bidimensionales e inteligencia artificial. Gracias a este avance, las personas ciegas podrán explorar esquemas, mapas y documentos digitales en tiempo real.

El proyecto ABILITY ( Accessible Digital Services for Blind and Partially Sighted People ) es una investigación financiada por la Unión Europea dentro del programa Horizonte Europa. Su objetivo principal es eliminar la brecha visual en el entorno digital.

Hasta ahora, las líneas braille convencionales solo muestran una fila de caracteres a la vez. Si un estudiante abre un libro de biología o un informe económico, el software solo puede leer una breve descripción escrita por el autor. Cuando esa descripción no existe, la información se pierde por completo. ABILITY resuelve este obstáculo permitiendo que el usuario sienta la forma real del contenido directamente bajo sus dedos.

Para lograr que una imagen compleja tenga sentido al tacto, no basta con levantar puntos al azar. Una fotografía o un gráfico saturado de líneas resultaría confuso para la yema de los dedos. Por ello, el sistema funciona en tres fases coordinadas:

Análisis mediante visión por computador: Primero, la inteligencia artificial escanea el archivo digital, web o presentación. El algoritmo identifica qué elementos son relevantes y elimina el ruido visual innecesario.

Traducción a vectores táctiles: A continuación, el software simplifica la imagen y la envía a una tableta gráfica táctil de alta densidad. Esta superficie eleva pequeños pines físicos en tiempo real, dibujando el contorno del mapa o la curva del gráfico.

Interacción multimodal con audio: Finalmente, el sistema combina el tacto con la voz. Cuando la persona desliza su dedo por un punto concreto de la pantalla, el dispositivo lee en voz alta el dato exacto o la etiqueta de esa zona.

El concepto de las pantallas táctiles gráficas no es nuevo en el sector. Dispositivos comerciales como Graphiti o Canute ya demostraron su utilidad hace años. No obstante, su precio —que oscila entre los 3.000 y los 15.000 euros— los convierte en herramientas inalcanzables para la mayoría de los hogares.

Uno de los pilares del proyecto ABILITY es precisamente la democratización económica. El consorcio europeo, en el que participan centros de referencia como la Universidad Johannes Kepler de Linz y empresas especializadas como Inventivio, trabaja con nuevos materiales y actuadores más económicos. De este modo, buscan que esta tecnología llegue tanto a colegios y universidades como a puestos de trabajo cotidianos.

La llegada de soluciones como ABILITY abre la puerta a una verdadera igualdad de oportunidades en ámbitos académicos y profesionales. Hasta hoy, cursar ingeniería, matemáticas, economía o arquitectura exigía depender de impresoras especiales de relieve (como los hornos Fuser) y esperar semanas para recibir el material adaptado.

Con esta nueva generación de tabletas táctiles inteligentes, cualquier alumno ciego podrá descargar los apuntes en clase y explorar los mismos diagramas que sus compañeros al instante. La tiflotecnología da así un paso gigante hacia una accesibilidad universal real, autónoma y sin esperas.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuentes: CORDIS EU Research Results – ABILITY Project , ABILITY Project Official Website , Instituto de Informática Integrada de la Universidad Johannes Kepler

news.title: Guest House
news.summary: Guest House: a free Mac app for running Windows and Linux with VoiceOver, no sighted help Hi everyone, I want to tell you about a free Mac app called Guest House. A friend of mine, Amena Thomas, develops it, so I'm not neutral, but I think a lot of people here will want to know it exists. Guest House sets up and runs virtual machines on a Mac, and it is built for VoiceOver users from the start. You can install Windows 11 without sighted help at any step. The app speaks what it is doing through VoiceOver, and when something goes wrong it tells you what happened and what to do next. What it does: - **Windows 11 for ARM:** Guest House can download Windows straight from Microsoft, answer the setup questions for you, and install it. - **A screen reader from the first sign-in:** it can install NVDA for you, and JAWS if you choose it. JAWS needs your own license. - **Linux:** Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Kali, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux and openSUSE Tumbleweed install with no installer questions, with Orca speaking from the first boot. - **macOS:** it can also run macOS virtual machines. - **Braille displays:** you can pass a USB braille display through to Windows. - **Windows apps in Command-Tab:** your Windows apps can appear in the Mac's app switcher. - **Control-Alt keys with VoiceOver on:** VoiceOver keeps Control-Option for itself, so you hold Command-Option instead. Command-Option-Right Arrow reaches Windows as Control-Alt-Right Arrow. - **Everyday extras:** copy and paste between the Mac and Windows, a shared folder, restore points, and a list of Windows apps it can install for you. What you should know: - It needs a Mac with Apple silicon. It does not run on Intel Macs. - It is free and open source, under the GPL version 2. - It is still in early testing, so you may find bugs. Help > Report a Problem puts a report on the clipboard and opens a new issue for you to paste it into. - It grew out of Allison Meloy's Accessible Virtual Machine, and builds on her work. I have been testing this and Amena has been incredibly responsive fixing a show-stopping issue for my specific use case very quickly once reported. She is keen for any feedback so please don't hesitate to get in touch. You can download it and read more here: https://fullcircleat.com/guest-house/
news.body:
Guest House: a free Mac app for running Windows and Linux with VoiceOver, no sighted help

Hi everyone,

I want to tell you about a free Mac app called Guest House. A friend of mine, Amena Thomas, develops it, so I'm not neutral, but I think a lot of people here will want to know it exists.

Guest House sets up and runs virtual machines on a Mac, and it is built for VoiceOver users from the start. You can install Windows 11 without sighted help at any step. The app speaks what it is doing through VoiceOver, and when something goes wrong it tells you what happened and what to do next.

What it does:

- **Windows 11 for ARM:** Guest House can download Windows straight from Microsoft, answer the setup questions for you, and install it. - **A screen reader from the first sign-in:** it can install NVDA for you, and JAWS if you choose it. JAWS needs your own license. - **Linux:** Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Kali, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux and openSUSE Tumbleweed install with no installer questions, with Orca speaking from the first boot. - **macOS:** it can also run macOS virtual machines. - **Braille displays:** you can pass a USB braille display through to Windows. - **Windows apps in Command-Tab:** your Windows apps can appear in the Mac's app switcher. - **Control-Alt keys with VoiceOver on:** VoiceOver keeps Control-Option for itself, so you hold Command-Option instead. Command-Option-Right Arrow reaches Windows as Control-Alt-Right Arrow. - **Everyday extras:** copy and paste between the Mac and Windows, a shared folder, restore points, and a list of Windows apps it can install for you.

What you should know:

- It needs a Mac with Apple silicon. It does not run on Intel Macs. - It is free and open source, under the GPL version 2. - It is still in early testing, so you may find bugs. Help > Report a Problem puts a report on the clipboard and opens a new issue for you to paste it into. - It grew out of Allison Meloy's Accessible Virtual Machine, and builds on her work. I have been testing this and Amena has been incredibly responsive fixing a show-stopping issue for my specific use case very quickly once reported. She is keen for any feedback so please don't hesitate to get in touch. You can download it and read more here: https://fullcircleat.com/guest-house/

news.title: Twangle: Guitar Tuner
news.summary: Twangle is a free tuner for guitar, bass, ukulele, violin, viola, cello, mandolin and banjo, with a chromatic mode for any other instrument or your…
news.body:
Published 17 November 2026 by Klaboukes

Twangle is a free tuner for guitar, bass, ukulele, violin, viola, cello, mandolin and banjo, with a chromatic mode for any other instrument or your voice. Play a string and it tells you the note and how far off it is, in cents.

Besides tuning it has a metronome with tap tempo and a speed trainer, chord charts, scales, a capo helper and ear training. Every feature is free: no ads, no purchases, no account. Twangle has no internet permission at all, so the sound from the microphone is analysed on the phone and never recorded or sent anywhere. It is available in 36 languages.

I’m the developer. The code is written with Claude, an AI by Anthropic, to my design, and I test every version myself on real phones.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Twangle was made to work fully with TalkBack, and I’d like blind and low-vision players to tell me whether it does. Tuner: TalkBack reads the result in words, for example “E 2, 12 cents flat, tighten” or “F sharp 2, in tune”. To avoid constant chatter it waits 0.4 seconds before saying a new note, and it doesn’t announce small changes in cents. The tuner ignores TalkBack’s own voice, so speech doesn’t trigger a false reading. String buttons are labelled (“A 2, selected”); hold one to hear its note and tune by ear. The strum check tells you how many strings are in tune (“4 of 6 in tune”). Vibration guide: on by default while TalkBack is running (Settings, While tuning, Vibration guide). While the tuner hears a string, one tap means tighten and two taps mean loosen. The taps come faster as you get closer, and one long buzz means in tune. The taps make no sound, so they don’t disturb the tuner. More at https://klaboukes.github.io/help.html#without-looking Other tools: chord charts and scales are read string by string (“A 2 string, fret 3, finger 3, C”). The metronome’s tempo is an adjustable slider, and it can vibrate on the beat. Ear training answers are buttons with names. The metronome and the practice tools work without microphone permission. Low vision: there is a high-contrast look (pure black and white, thicker lines, at least 7:1 contrast), turned on automatically when the phone’s high-contrast text is on. Every screen works with text at twice the normal size. Known issue: in the Chords screen, the selected chord root is shown with a grey fill and a thicker edge rather than full contrast. I’m sighted. Every screen’s TalkBack labels are checked by automated tests, and I tested it with TalkBack myself on on a Samsung Galaxy S26 (Android 17) and a Xiaomi 12X (Android 13).. I’d really value answers to two questions: while you tune, what works best for you: speech, vibration, or sounds such as ticks (with earbuds)? And for low-vision players: what does the high-contrast look lack?

Last Tested App version and Android version:

Twangle 2.2.0, on a Samsung Galaxy S26 (Android 17) and a Xiaomi 12X (Android 13).

No accessibility ratings yet. Be the first to rate this app.

Please use this rating only for accessibility. For feedback about the app’s features, price, overall quality, or your general experience, use the comments section below.

Please log in to rate this app’s accessibility.

news.title: ViTrack: cámaras con inteligencia artificial para ayudar a las personas ciegas a orientarse
news.summary: La orientación y la movilidad siguen siendo dos de los grandes retos para las personas ciegas y con discapacidad visual. Aunque existen herramientas como el bastón blanco, las aplicaciones de navegación GPS y los dispositivos de asistencia electrónica, desplazarse por entornos desconocidos o detectar obstáculos puede resultar complicado, especialmente en espacios donde las tecnologías de […] La entrada ViTrack: cámaras con inteligencia artificial para ayudar a las personas ciegas a orientarse se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
La orientación y la movilidad siguen siendo dos de los grandes retos para las personas ciegas y con discapacidad visual. Aunque existen herramientas como el bastón blanco, las aplicaciones de navegación GPS y los dispositivos de asistencia electrónica, desplazarse por entornos desconocidos o detectar obstáculos puede resultar complicado, especialmente en espacios donde las tecnologías de posicionamiento convencionales no funcionan correctamente.

En este contexto, investigadores de la Universidad Nacional Cheng Kung (NCKU), en Taiwán, han desarrollado ViTrack , un sistema experimental que combina inteligencia artificial, cámaras de vigilancia y tecnología inalámbrica Bluetooth para facilitar la orientación de personas con discapacidad visual.

La propuesta destaca por aprovechar infraestructuras que ya existen en muchos edificios y espacios públicos, como las cámaras de seguridad, evitando que el usuario tenga que llevar dispositivos adicionales para recibir asistencia durante sus desplazamientos.

El funcionamiento de ViTrack se basa en combinar dos tecnologías que habitualmente se utilizan por separado: el posicionamiento mediante señales inalámbricas y el análisis de imágenes mediante inteligencia artificial.

Por una parte, el sistema utiliza pequeños receptores inalámbricos que detectan las señales Bluetooth de un teléfono móvil. Estas señales permiten estimar la posición aproximada del usuario dentro de una zona determinada.

Por otra, las cámaras de vigilancia instaladas en el entorno proporcionan imágenes que son analizadas mediante algoritmos de visión artificial. De esta manera, el sistema puede identificar a la persona que ha solicitado asistencia, seguir sus movimientos y reconocer posibles obstáculos en su recorrido.

La combinación de ambas tecnologías permite obtener información más completa sobre la posición y la dirección de desplazamiento del usuario.

Uno de los aspectos más interesantes es que ViTrack utiliza una perspectiva externa, es decir, observa los desplazamientos desde las cámaras instaladas en el entorno en lugar de depender exclusivamente de una cámara situada en el cuerpo o en unas gafas inteligentes.

ViTrack no se limita a localizar al usuario. También incorpora funciones destinadas a ayudarle a mantener una trayectoria determinada y detectar situaciones que pueden dificultar su desplazamiento.

El sistema analiza la orientación corporal de la persona y la compara con la dirección que debería seguir. Si detecta que se está desviando del recorrido previsto, puede generar indicaciones para corregir la trayectoria.

Además, los algoritmos de visión artificial permiten identificar obstáculos situados en el camino, como una bicicleta estacionada sobre una zona de paso.

La información se transforma en avisos de orientación que pueden enviarse al teléfono móvil del usuario mediante indicaciones acústicas. Entre las instrucciones contempladas se encuentran indicaciones para continuar recto, girar a la izquierda o a la derecha, así como alertas cuando se detectan obstáculos.

Para realizar estas tareas, los investigadores emplean modelos de inteligencia artificial como YOLOv7, utilizado para la detección de objetos, y redes neuronales LSTM, que ayudan a interpretar las señales inalámbricas y estimar la posición del usuario.

Uno de los elementos diferenciadores de ViTrack es su planteamiento de reutilización de infraestructuras existentes.

En lugar de exigir la instalación de una red completamente nueva de sensores, el sistema pretende aprovechar las cámaras de vigilancia que ya están presentes en numerosos espacios públicos y edificios.

Esto podría facilitar su implantación en lugares como universidades, hospitales, estaciones de transporte o grandes instalaciones, siempre que dispongan de una infraestructura compatible y se realicen las adaptaciones necesarias.

Además, el usuario únicamente necesita llevar consigo un teléfono inteligente con Bluetooth activado para que el sistema pueda detectar su presencia y comenzar el proceso de seguimiento dentro de las zonas habilitadas.

Los investigadores también plantean un diseño orientado a proteger la privacidad, mediante un sistema de activación controlado por el usuario y el aprovechamiento de redes de cámaras existentes.

ViTrack es todavía una investigación experimental. El trabajo, publicado en febrero de 2026 en la revista científica Multimedia Tools and Applications , describe el desarrollo y la evaluación de un prototipo utilizando la infraestructura de vigilancia de la Universidad Nacional Cheng Kung.

La demostración se realizó en una zona exterior del campus, donde los investigadores utilizaron una cámara para supervisar un tramo de aproximadamente 16 metros de pavimento podotáctil. El recorrido incluía diferentes puntos de referencia y posibles obstáculos.

Las pruebas permitieron evaluar la capacidad del sistema para identificar al usuario, estimar su posición, detectar desviaciones respecto al itinerario y reconocer obstáculos.

Los resultados muestran que la combinación de Bluetooth y visión artificial puede mejorar la localización y el seguimiento respecto al uso aislado de las señales inalámbricas.

No obstante, los propios investigadores reconocen que todavía es necesario ampliar las pruebas a entornos más complejos, con mayor número de personas y situaciones de movilidad más dinámicas. También plantean realizar nuevas evaluaciones con personas con discapacidad visual para comprobar su utilidad en condiciones reales de uso.

La principal aportación de ViTrack es explorar una alternativa a los sistemas de navegación que dependen exclusivamente de dispositivos que el usuario debe llevar consigo.

Su planteamiento permite trasladar parte de la tecnología de asistencia al propio entorno, utilizando cámaras y sensores para proporcionar información sobre los desplazamientos.

Sin embargo, su desarrollo también plantea cuestiones importantes: la necesidad de contar con cámaras y receptores compatibles, la cobertura de las zonas supervisadas, la protección de los datos personales y la fiabilidad de las indicaciones cuando aparecen obstáculos imprevistos.

Por tanto, ViTrack no pretende sustituir herramientas fundamentales como el bastón blanco ni la formación en orientación y movilidad. Su interés reside en estudiar cómo la inteligencia artificial y las infraestructuras inteligentes pueden convertirse en recursos complementarios para mejorar la autonomía personal.

La investigación abre una vía interesante para el futuro de la tiflotecnología: desarrollar entornos capaces de proporcionar información accesible y asistencia a las personas con discapacidad visual sin que toda la tecnología tenga que estar incorporada en un dispositivo portátil.

Fuentes: Springer Nature Link , Research NCKU .

news.title: LiDAR en los teléfonos móviles: una tecnología que podría ayudar a las personas ciegas a detectar escaleras y desniveles
news.summary: Los avances en tiflotecnología no siempre requieren desarrollar nuevos dispositivos. En ocasiones, el potencial está en aprovechar tecnologías que ya incorporan herramientas de uso cotidiano, como los teléfonos inteligentes. Es el caso del sistema experimental desarrollado por investigadores de la Universidad de Iowa (Estados Unidos), que utiliza el sensor LiDAR de un teléfono móvil para […] La entrada LiDAR en los teléfonos móviles: una tecnología que podría ayudar a las personas ciegas a detectar escaleras y desniveles se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
Los avances en tiflotecnología no siempre requieren desarrollar nuevos dispositivos. En ocasiones, el potencial está en aprovechar tecnologías que ya incorporan herramientas de uso cotidiano, como los teléfonos inteligentes.

Es el caso del sistema experimental desarrollado por investigadores de la Universidad de Iowa (Estados Unidos), que utiliza el sensor LiDAR de un teléfono móvil para detectar escaleras y cambios de altura en el terreno en tiempo real.

La investigación, publicada el 2 de octubre de 2026 en la revista científica Scientific Reports , demuestra que es posible utilizar el sensor de profundidad de un smartphone comercial para identificar determinados riesgos durante los desplazamientos, sin necesidad de incorporar cámaras externas ni hardware especializado.

LiDAR es una tecnología que permite medir distancias y obtener información tridimensional del entorno mediante pulsos de luz láser.

Algunos teléfonos inteligentes, como determinados modelos de iPhone Pro, incorporan sensores LiDAR que permiten detectar la profundidad de los objetos y construir representaciones tridimensionales de los espacios.

Aunque esta tecnología se utiliza habitualmente en fotografía, aplicaciones de realidad aumentada y mediciones de espacios, también ofrece posibilidades interesantes en el ámbito de la accesibilidad.

En este caso, los investigadores han aprovechado esa capacidad para identificar irregularidades en el suelo, especialmente escaleras y cambios de altura que pueden pasar desapercibidos durante los desplazamientos de una persona ciega o con baja visión.

El sistema desarrollado utiliza un iPhone 17 Pro Max con iOS 26.2 y el sensor LiDAR integrado en el dispositivo.

Su funcionamiento se basa en analizar la representación tridimensional del entorno que genera el teléfono. A partir de esa información, un algoritmo proyecta ocho líneas virtuales en diferentes direcciones para identificar cambios geométricos en la superficie.

Cuando detecta una variación compatible con una escalera o un desnivel, el sistema puede generar una alerta para advertir al usuario.

Una de las características más interesantes es que el procesamiento se realiza directamente en el teléfono, sin necesidad de enviar las imágenes a servidores externos ni utilizar procesamiento en la nube.

El algoritmo analiza la información a una frecuencia de 60 imágenes por segundo, lo que permite detectar cambios en el entorno con una respuesta prácticamente inmediata.

Para comprobar el funcionamiento del sistema, los investigadores realizaron 120 pruebas en ocho ubicaciones diferentes, utilizando escaleras con distintas alturas y pendientes.

Los ensayos contemplaron diferentes condiciones de iluminación, tanto en interiores como en exteriores, y aproximaciones a las escaleras desde arriba y desde abajo.

Los resultados fueron los siguientes:

Los investigadores también observaron diferencias según la dirección de aproximación. La detección fue menos eficaz cuando el usuario se acercaba a las escaleras desde arriba, algo especialmente relevante porque los desniveles descendentes pueden resultar difíciles de identificar mediante sensores de profundidad.

Es importante interpretar estos resultados con cautela: las pruebas fueron realizadas por un único operador entrenado y no incluyeron participantes ciegos o con baja visión. Además, no se llevaron a cabo ensayos específicos en recorridos sin obstáculos para establecer una tasa de falsas alarmas fiable.

Por tanto, los resultados demuestran la viabilidad técnica del sistema, pero todavía no permiten afirmar que esté preparado para su utilización autónoma en situaciones reales.

Una de las ventajas de esta investigación es que no requiere desarrollar un dispositivo completamente nuevo.

El sistema aprovecha un sensor LiDAR que ya está integrado en determinados teléfonos comerciales. Esto abre la posibilidad de explorar aplicaciones de asistencia visual utilizando hardware que algunas personas ya tienen a su disposición.

No obstante, es importante señalar que no todos los smartphones incorporan LiDAR. Además, el algoritmo desarrollado depende de las características del sensor y del entorno de programación utilizado, por lo que no puede trasladarse automáticamente a cualquier teléfono.

Los investigadores consideran necesario ampliar las pruebas, incorporar diferentes dispositivos y evaluar el funcionamiento del sistema con personas ciegas y con baja visión antes de plantear su utilización como herramienta de movilidad.

La detección de escaleras y desniveles continúa siendo uno de los desafíos de la movilidad para las personas con discapacidad visual.

Aunque el bastón blanco es una herramienta fundamental para detectar obstáculos y explorar el espacio próximo, determinadas situaciones pueden requerir información adicional sobre las características del terreno.

La utilización de sensores de profundidad en teléfonos móviles podría abrir nuevas posibilidades para complementar las ayudas técnicas existentes, proporcionando información adicional sobre el entorno y anticipando determinados riesgos.

Sin embargo, estas tecnologías todavía necesitan demostrar su fiabilidad en condiciones reales y no deben considerarse sustitutas del bastón blanco ni de la formación en orientación y movilidad.

La investigación demuestra que los sensores LiDAR de los teléfonos inteligentes tienen un potencial que va mucho más allá de la fotografía y la realidad aumentada. Su aplicación en el ámbito de la tiflotecnología podría contribuir al desarrollo de herramientas más accesibles, económicas y fáciles de integrar en dispositivos cotidianos.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuentes: Estudio científico completo

news.title: PLOT: AI Interactive Fiction
news.summary: PLOT is interactive fiction written by AI. Pick a genre, or write one line about the story you want, and the AI writes a scene.…
news.body:
Published 15 November 2026 by KihaKwon

PLOT is interactive fiction written by AI. Pick a genre, or write one line about the story you want, and the AI writes a scene. At the end of each scene you choose one of two options or type what happens next, and the story keeps going for as long as you like.

You can keep several stories going at once. Sign-in options include Google, Apple, Kakao, or a 6-digit email code. The app and stories are available in 40 languages.

PLOT is free with optional in-app purchases. You receive 30 pages at sign-up, can earn up to 49 additional one-time pages from first-step activities in the app, and can earn up to 17 pages per day through daily check-ins and small tasks. Optional short video ads can provide 3 pages each, up to 10 times per day. One page equals one scene.

One-time page packs are also available for purchase. There is no subscription and no banner advertising.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Disclosure: I’m the developer (Mirror Lab). I’ve used PLOT with TalkBack and my eyes closed on my Galaxy S25, for a long time last summer and again after 2.0. Just before 2.0.0, the main flow was also tested on a Galaxy S23 running Android 16, from sign-in to Get pages. No step got stuck.

PLOT follows system font size up to 200%, bold font, high contrast text, and remove animations. PLOT does not read aloud by itself.

Version 2.0.1 fixes these three issues and was in Google Play review in November 2026. The keyboard fix requires Android 15 or later. Video ads have not yet been checked with TalkBack.

Feedback is welcome, including workarounds you may have found. Contact contact@plotai.app , or use Profile > Settings > Feedback & support in the app.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

PLOT 2.0.0, Android 16 (Samsung Galaxy S23)

news.title: AcessGallery
news.summary: AcessGallery is a photo and video gallery built from the ground up for blind and low-vision people who use a screen reader. Instead of simply…
news.body:
Published 14 November 2026 by Marco Rafael

AcessGallery is a photo and video gallery built from the ground up for blind and low-vision people who use a screen reader. Instead of simply announcing “Image” and a date, it uses AI to describe what is in your photos, narrate what happens in your videos, read text found in pictures, and answer your questions about any image.

The app also works as a complete gallery, with albums, a photos/videos filter, and support for Android’s “Open with” option. There are no ads and no account to create. The AI features use the Google Gemini API and can be enabled in two ways: with your own free API key, which is stored only on your device, or with the optional Facilitator plan, a monthly subscription for people who cannot or prefer not to create a key.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

I am the developer of AcessGallery. The app was designed for screen reader users from the start and every screen was tested with TalkBack. All buttons and controls have descriptive labels, state changes—such as a description finishing or a filter being applied—are announced, and touch targets are large to make them easy to find and activate.

With TalkBack, you can move through your photos and videos with standard gestures, double-tap a photo, and then ask for a description, have its text read aloud, or ask a question about it.

To use the AI features, you can create a free Gemini API key in Google AI Studio and paste it into the app’s settings. Since this setup can be difficult for less experienced users, the Facilitator plan offers a simpler alternative: subscribe and the AI features work right away, with no key to create or configure.

The AI features require an internet connection, and images are sent for processing by Google’s Gemini service. Face detection runs entirely on the device.

news.title: Easy Voice
news.summary: Easy Voice is a free text-to-speech routing app for Android. It does not synthesize speech itself; instead, it sits between Android and the TTS engines…
news.body:
Published 14 November 2026 by Syed Sharib Ali

Easy Voice is a free text-to-speech routing app for Android. It does not synthesize speech itself; instead, it sits between Android and the TTS engines already installed on the device, routing text to the engine best suited to the detected language and selected mode.

Dual Languages Mode uses a primary and secondary language, routing Latin-script text through the primary language and matching non-Latin text to the configured secondary engine.

Auto Language Mode can use as many configured languages as needed and sends each complete block of text to a single matching engine.

Mixed Mode processes words and languages with their own configured TTS engines, making it better suited to content that frequently switches languages.

Easy Voice also includes advanced options for smart number processing, punctuation handling, quick character reading, accessibility-volume output, and Keep Alive behavior.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Setting up Easy Voice takes only a few minutes. Follow these steps:

The Configurations tab gives you detailed control over every language. You can enable, disable, or remove languages at any time. There is also a checkbox that invokes the corresponding TTS engine immediately, with no delay. This is especially useful when a TTS engine supports only one language.

The Advanced tab offers several options for tuning how Easy Voice behaves:

news.title: Use Photo Tracking in ZoomText to Jump to the Objects in a Picture
news.summary: Have you ever opened a photo and wanted to know right away who’s in it, or spot the dog in the corner, or see what’s on the dinner plate? If you use magnification, you know how that usually goes. You zoom in, pan across the picture bit by bit, and hope you don’t miss what …
news.body:
Have you ever opened a photo and wanted to know right away who’s in it, or spot the dog in the corner, or see what’s on the dinner plate? If you use magnification, you know how that usually goes. You zoom in, pan across the picture bit by bit, and hope you don’t miss what you’re looking for. It works, but it takes time and patience.

Photo Tracking, new in ZoomText 2027, makes this much easier. Instead of scanning every corner of an image, you can go straight to the things that matter to you. Let’s take a look at what it does and how to get started.

Photo Tracking identifies people, animals, food, and other objects in an image. Then it moves the magnified view directly from one object to the next. You no longer need to zoom and pan across the whole picture to find what you want. Photo Tracking takes you right to it.

Photo Tracking is available in ZoomText Magnifier/Reader, ZoomText Magnifier, and Fusion.

Pictures are everywhere: on web pages, in Word documents and PDFs, and in your own photo collection. Photo Tracking helps you get to the parts of an image you care about quickly, so you spend less time searching and more time enjoying or using what you find.

There’s another big benefit. All recognition happens locally on your computer. That means Photo Tracking works offline, and it’s suitable for secure environments where images can’t be sent to an online service.

Getting started takes just a few steps:

Tip: You can also set Photo Tracking to analyze the active window automatically.

Photo Tracking sorts the objects it finds into ten categories:

It starts with your favorite categories, which are Animals and People by default. If you’d rather start somewhere else, you can change your favorites in Photo Tracking Settings.

Use these keystrokes while you explore an image:

When you zoom in or out with CAPS LOCK+UP ARROW , CAPS LOCK+DOWN ARROW , or CAPS LOCK+ENTER while using Photo Tracking, ZoomText announces the new magnification level, so you always know where you are.

For complete hotkeys and settings, see the Photo Tracking help topic in ZoomText. To learn more about Photo Tracking and other ZoomText 2027 features, visit What’s New in ZoomText 2027 .

Give Photo Tracking a try the next time you come across a picture. We think you’ll enjoy how quickly you can find what you’re looking for.

Have questions? Send an email to training@vispero.com .

news.title: In-Process 13th November 2026
news.summary: This week, we’ve updated NVDA, and some documentation, we hear from our user group in Japan, plus there are tips for File Explorer and more! NVDA 2026.3.1 Updated VPAT / ACR NVDA on show in Japan Unassigned gestures File Explorer shortcuts NVDA 2026.3.1 NV Access is pleased to announce that version 2026.3.1 of NVDA, the… Read More
news.body:
This week, we’ve updated NVDA, and some documentation, we hear from our user group in Japan, plus there are tips for File Explorer and more!

NV Access is pleased to announce that version 2026.3.1 of NVDA , the free screen reader for Microsoft Windows, is now available for download. We encourage all users to upgrade to this version.

Highlights This is a patch release to fix security issues. A bug fix is also included for an issue introduced in 2026.3 with the task switcher in Windows 10. The Brazilian Portuguese eSpeak voice was restored to the behaviour in 2026.2.

Read the full changes and download at the NVDA 2026.3.1 release announcement .

We’ve updated our VPAT. Actually we’ve updated our ACR , but whatever you call it, there’s a new one. Mostly of interest to companies who use NVDA and need to keep a copy on file for any software they use, the activity of completing it is useful, even for us as a screen reader manufacturer. VPAT stands for Voluntary Product Accessibility Template – it’s a large document which gives you points to consider and rate your software and website on many aspects of accessibility. VPAT is technically the blank template. The Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) is the completed report about a product.

NVDA is, as you would expect, quite good at all the things someone who is blind might need. However, through this process, over the years, we have previously identified and fixed several issues which may affect other users. The newest version of this document doesn’t dramatically change any of our ratings or identify or fix any new issues, but it is up to date for NVDA 2026.3.1. So, if your organisation needs a copy, head over to the VPAT section of the Corporate and Government page and you’ll find it there.

We love to hear from our communities all around the world. There is a very active community of users, and contributors in Japan. They have a website devoted to the local community: https://www.nvda.jp/ and recently attended the Sight World 2026 conference in Tokyo https://www.sight-world.com/sightworld2026

Nobuyuki and the team presented at the conference on four main themes: Screen sharing using Copilot Add-on Store NVDA Coach New Forms of Learning with NVDA

They wrote to advise us that the event was a huge success, and they had around 100 people in attendance at their presentation. They sent us photographs and a link to their video presentation:

The Video is in Japanese, and includes a message from NV Access Training & Support manager Quentin Christensen (in English).

A banner from the NVDA Japanese Team session titled “NVDAではじめる、新しい「学び」のかたち” (“A New Form of ‘Learning’ Starting with NVDA”), presented at Sight World 2026 in Tokyo.

Unassigned gestures The last couple of releases I’ve highlighted the unassigned gestures, so let’s do that again. Unassigned gestures are things which you can do with a keystroke or touch action etc, but we didn’t set one up by default. There are only two this time around: Magnifier: A new unassigned command has been added to move the mouse cursor to the center of the magnified view. Added an unassigned Quick Navigation Command for jumping to the next/previous clickable element in browse mode.

The magnifier command is thanks to Cyrille, and the clickable one thanks to Cary. Thank you to them and ALL of our amazing NVDA community contributors!

One of the fixes in NVDA 2026.3.1 is with reporting switching Windows in Windows 10. I was thinking of writing a post on using alt+tab and the other ways of switching Windows – there are a few! But I realised, I already wrote a piece on switching Windows .

I’d forgotten about alt+escape ; I’m going to get back into using that! But that got me thinking about other general Windows keystrokes we might not know or (like me) might have forgotten. Another recent fix in NVDA (from NVDA 2026.3) is with File Explorer, so I thought we’d have a look at a couple of shortcuts which are well worth knowing, and some you may find useful:

Firstly, to start File Explorer, press Windows+e Open a new File Explorer window (from within File Explorer), with control+n

Navigating Move to next area: tab Move to previous area: shift+tab The focus starts in the “Items view list” – the contents of the currently selected folder. From here: Press shift+tab once to the folder list (you had to press it twice in some versions). Press tab to the “Split button” which is the name of the field the item list is sorted on. Once on the split button, use the arrows to select a field and enter or space to sort on it – if you select the same field, it will reverse the sort).

When in the items list view, you can customise the view. Windows provides shortcuts for the various views: control+shift+1 : Extra-large icons control+shift+2 : Large icons control+shift+3 : Medium icons control+shift+4 : Small icons control+shift+5 : List view control+shift+6 : Details view control+shift+7 : Tiles control+shift+8 : Content Note that in some versions of Windows (such as recent builds of Windows 11) these shortcuts do NOT work, but control+ALT+number works, for instance control+alt+6 for details view. The “details” view is the one I would personally recommend, as everything is in one list, and you get the most information about each item (file type, size, date modified etc) and can sort on any of those fields as needed. In details view, use the up and down arrow keys to move through the list. In most other view types, e.g. the icons views, use the left and right arrow keys .

Tabs Like browsers, you can have multiple folders open in different tabs or different windows: New blank tab: control+t Move to next tab: control+tab Move to previous tab: control+shift+tab

I cannot find a keystroke to open the current folder in a new tab. If you know one, please let me know! In the meantime, the following would work: Press shift+f6 once from the folder list to move to the tab control list. Press the applications key (or shift+f10 ) to open the context menu. Press the up arrow once to “Duplicate tab”. Press enter to open a new tab with the current folder.

To close a tab without closing all the other tabs, press control+w .

Address bar Move the focus to the address bar: alt+d . On the address bar, you can type the name of the folder or paste it from elsewhere, then press enter to load that folder.

Windows has several special folders. If you email us for help with an issue, we might ask you to send us your NVDA log, which you can find in your %temp% folder. To get to your %temp% folder: In File Explorer, press alt+d to go to the address bar Type: %temp% (That is, the word ‘temp’ with a percent sign either side) Press enter Windows will load a folder such as C:\Users\YourName\AppData\Local\Temp which is where it is storing your temporary files. There are others such as %onedrive% for your OneDrive folder (if setup), as well as system folders which are worth being careful around.

File properties One other quirk in File Explorer is opening file properties. In the file list, once you have located a file, press alt+enter to open the file properties for that file. This only works from the file list, even though you can access “ Properties ” in the context menu on folders in the folder list and it notes the alt+enter shortcut.

That’s all for this fortnight. We’ll be back towards the end of the month with more news, tips and tricks. I’m not sure what will be in that edition, but after all those lists of things in the file manager section, I’m going to aim for zero lists next fortnight – keep an eye out for that to see if I can do it!

Do keep the conversation going in the NVDA users email group , and remember, if you’d like to receive this blog by email, you can! Just go to https://www.nvaccess.org/newsletter and you can sign up for the blog, for details as new versions of NVDA drop, and more.

news.title: Navia: AI Accessible Map
news.summary: Navia is a touchable offline map for blind and low-vision people. Slide a finger across the screen and Navia speaks the street, shop, or place…
news.body:
Published 12 November 2026 by Mohammad

Navia is a touchable offline map for blind and low-vision people. Slide a finger across the screen and Navia speaks the street, shop, or place under your finger: its name, what it is, how far away it is, and directions as clock positions (for example, “2 o’clock, 40 meters”), following the way O&M training teaches. Sweeping around the map lets you build a mental picture of an area before you go there.

Safety note: Navia is an extra aid only. Always use a cane, guide dog, or another safe mobility method first.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

I am the developer. Navia was designed around TalkBack from the start rather than adapted afterwards. All buttons and controls are labelled and every dialog can be read with TalkBack.

The map itself is explored by touch: with TalkBack on, sliding a finger over the map speaks what is under it, and double-tap opens a menu of actions for that place (aim, hear its sounds, open in Google Maps, add to favourites). Voice dictation is available for search, adding points and renaming places.

For low vision there is an optional drawn map with a different marker shape per kind of place (not colour alone), street labels and a light/dark theme; it can turn itself off while TalkBack is running. Tested with Google TalkBack, including automated tests that run with real TalkBack enabled.

Known limitations: AI place recognition is experimental, needs a one-time ~240 MB model download and can miss a place; map quality depends on OpenStreetMap coverage in your area. Feedback is very welcome.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

Navia 1.1.12. Android 15
